## The data $\times$ analysis matrix

```{r}
#| label: matrix
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
repeatability_matrix()
```

::: {.src}
@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen; @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms
:::

::: notes
The grid holds that vocabulary, and if you take one thing home, I would like it to be this grid. The question stays the same in every cell, while the data and the analysis vary. Reproducibility is the same data under the same analysis, and it asks whether rerunning the recipe gives the same number. Robustness keeps the data and replaces the analysis with another justifiable one, and asks whether the finding survives defensible choices made by someone else. Replicability applies the same analysis to new data. The fourth cell, new data under a new analysis, is generalisability, which we leave aside. Everything that follows refers back to this grid.
:::

## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.85; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms [p. 2]
:::

::: notes
The glossary separates two things that we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella term, reproducibility, robustness and replicability taken as a family, all asking whether the answer survives the repetition of some step of the research process. Credibility and trustworthiness concern how much confidence a finding deserves, and the sentence in the middle of the slide says that, because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth, so a credible finding can be wrong. Credibility is built from the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them, the last of which recurs throughout the day.
:::

## Quick check – the matrix in peer review {#quick-check-credibility-in-the-wild .questionslide transition="fade-in none-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

- 'Reviewer 1' wants to ensure that your results are [reproducible]{.fragment .bounceIn}, so she sources your R script to run the entire analysis. You're in luck – she hasn't yet updated her `dplyr`, so the code runs.
- 'Reviewer 2' is very eager. He's unconvinced by your modelling choices, so he fits your data to another function to check if your findings are truly [robust]{.fragment .bounceIn}. You're in luck again – he recovers your point estimate to a reasonable precision, although the confidence intervals have widened.
- 'Reviewer 3' takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?
:::

::: notes
This is the grid at work on one paper. You submit a paper with its replication package, and three reviewers each check something different. For each one, call out the cell of the grid in which that reviewer works, before the answer appears. Reviewer 1 reruns your own script on your own data. [pause] [advance] Reproduction. Reviewer 2 fits your data with a different function. [pause] [advance] Robustness. Reviewer 3 applies your methods to a dataset published by somebody else. [pause] [advance] Replication.
:::

## Quick check – the matrix in peer review {#quick-check-credibility-in-the-wild-1 .questionslide transition="none-in fade-out"}

::: {.none}
You submit your paper and replication package. It goes out to reviewers.

'Reviewer 2' just doesn't want to let go...

- He tried a few alternative analyses of your data, including a fancy new regression method that he just released as an R package. His method gives results that are generally aligned to yours, but for the method to work, it would require a larger dataset; would your results really [generalise]{.fragment .bounceIn} to this new dataset published by 'Reviewer 3' that he just read about, if applying his new fancy method to it?
:::

::: notes
Reviewer 2 has not finished. His new method agrees with your results, but it needs more data than you had, so he wants to run it on the dataset published by Reviewer 3, and I ask you again for the cell. [pause] [advance] New data under a new analysis put him in the fourth cell, generalisability. Each of these checks asks a different question of the same paper, and passing one of them does not settle the others.
:::

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start, your code, your data or your materials, and open research is a list of practices that supply them, each removing one identifiable obstacle. Open data lets someone else reanalyse your evidence, open code lets them rerun your exact analysis, and open materials let them run the study again in a new sample. Open access lets them read the paper at all, which sounds trivial until you try to obtain a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the analysis plan, filed before the results exist, and registered reports go further, since the plan is peer-reviewed and the decision to publish is taken before anyone has a result. [advance] None of these practices guards against every problem, and whether published findings hold up when somebody checks them has now been measured on a large scale.
:::
